channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Wikicity.app
item.description: Spotted on Reddit: Fly around a visualization of the 100,000 most popular Wikipedia pages represented as buildings. The more page views in the last 30 days, the higher the building. There’s an explore mode for, well, exploring, and a Fly mode where you can zoom around and knock over the buildings. (Sorry about that, Gary Oldman building.)

item.title: City Installs Benches At Ukrainian Village Bus Stops Where DIY Versions Popped Up Last Month
item.description: Block Club Chicago: “About a month after two homemade benches appeared at CTA bus stops in Ukrainian Village, the city in recent days has installed sanctioned ‘ad benches’ at each location. But the group behind the original benches says their work will continue elsewhere: They plan to build and install their DIY structures at other bench-less bus stops across the larger West Town and Humboldt Park areas in the coming weeks.” This article is a followup to an article I indexed on September 15..

item.title: After bankruptcy, he was banned from sports betting sites. Then he discovered Kalshi
item.description: NPR: “Kalshi and its main competitor, Polymarket, have launched aggressive nationwide advertising campaigns, including in states where online sports gambling is illegal. And since the sites have not sought approval by states, they do not follow state-mandated protections for people with gambling addictions who are most vulnerable to relapsing.”

item.title: ‘Digital Armies’ and Disinformation: How Big Tech Is Hitting Brazil’s Upcoming Election
item.description: Byline Times: “Far-right populists worldwide are using AI to bypass traditional media gatekeepers and spread disinformation at scale. Nowhere is that more true than Brazil, which has been rocked by political disinformation in recent years and is expected to face even more daunting challenges with the rise of generative AI. These concerns are now reaching an inflection point just days ahead of Brazil’s general election on October 4 — a contest that sits at the intersection of the race to influence democracy with AI and the race to control the technology itself.”

item.title: Meta’s Muse reportedly keeps files on everyone you love
item.description: Mashable: “Muse is reportedly compiling data on users’ family, friends, partners, colleagues, ‘collaborators,’ and other people they follow online. Furthermore, a “Relationships” loop runs every hour in the background on a user’s computer, which updates each person’s page, according to researchers with FutureSociety.”

item.title: Court throws out Google location data in robbery case
item.description: Jersey Vindicator: “A New Jersey appeals court ruled Friday that cellphone location data used to convict a man of several gas station robberies must be thrown out because police lacked probable cause to obtain it from Google.”

item.title: Dying Patients Are Inundated by Misinformation. My Dad Was One of Them.
item.description: New York Times: “As my dad was, patients today are inundated with misinformation spread by alternative-medicine practitioners, social media influencers and public figures. They are willing to experiment with unproven therapies, often at great physical or financial risk, in part because they want more personalized and empathetic care — an antidote to the famously harsh aspects of traditional medicine.”

item.title: The Museum of Flight to Begin Installation of Nearly 2,000 Solar Panels on Aviation Pavilion
item.description: Vintage Aviation News: “The Museum of Flight in Seattle is launching a major sustainability initiative with the installation of 1,863 solar panels on the roof of its Aviation Pavilion. Beginning Oct. 5, the project is expected to generate enough electricity to meet 100 percent of the annual energy needs of the museum’s West Campus while reducing operating costs and supporting long-term environmental goals.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: American Library Association marks 150th Anniversary during Banned Books Week with list of 150 Most Challenged Books
item.description: American Library Association: “To mark the occasion and ALA’s official 150th anniversary on Oct. 6, ALA has released a list of the 150 most challenged books documented from 1990 through 2025. ALA’s Office for Intellectual Freedom tracked 4,235 unique titles challenged in 2025, the second-highest total on record. The full list of 150 most challenged books, available at ala150.org/150books spans contemporary titles such as Gender Queer: A Memoir by Maia Kobabe and literary classics such as To Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee and Of Mice and Men by John Steinbeck.”

item.title: VMFA Restores Ownership of Work by Enslaved Artist David Drake
item.description: Virginia Museum of Fine Arts: “The Virginia Museum of Fine Arts (VMFA) has reached a historic agreement with the descendants of enslaved artist David Drake (ca. 1800–ca. 1870) regarding his 1840 stoneware storage jug also known as a ‘poem’ vessel. VMFA has restored ownership of Double-handled Jug to Drake’s descendants and will purchase it back for the museum’s permanent collection in return for an authorized certificate of ethical ownership.”

item.title: Her Brand Was Tradwife. Now She’s Divorced.
item.description: New York Times: “Last year, [Bernadine] Bluntly left her husband and got a restraining order against him. A Missouri court found that she had proved allegations of domestic violence, and forbade him to come within 300 feet of her. (In a court filing, he denied committing “any act or pattern of domestic violence.”) After their divorce was finalized this past spring, she posted a video titled “What I Got Wrong About the Trad Movement.” It signaled a new life for her, and a new job: as an ex-tradwife influencer, warning women away from what she now describes as a program of spiritual manipulation and covert marital abuse.”

item.title: Mormon leader decries explosion in sports betting, prediction markets
item.description: Associated Press: “A leader of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints warned Saturday that an explosion in gambling driven by online prediction markets and sports betting is fostering greed, particularly among youths, while producing ‘nothing of value.'”

item.title: Rare images of Dallas history to be digitized through Sixth Floor Museum project
item.description: NBCDFW: “The Sixth Floor Museum at Dealey Plaza has received a $200,000-plus federal grant to preserve and digitize more than 20,000 photographs and related materials from Pulitzer Prize-winning photojournalist Bob Jackson. The two-year Museums for America grant from the Institute of Museum and Library Services will fund research, cataloging, and digitization of the Bob Jackson Collection, which documents Dallas history from 1960 to 1978.”

item.title: Apple and Google push states to shield app stores from some lawsuits
item.description: Politico: “Google and Apple lobbyists are engaged in a massive effort to press state lawmakers to adopt kids’ online safety laws that would shield the tech giants from some lawsuits tied to age-verification requirements, POLITICO has learned.”

item.title: Tate brothers used ‘lover boy’ model to exploit women, Britain says
item.description: Reuters: ” Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate used a ‘lover boy’ model to lure women with the ‌promise of romantic relationships before coercing them to create online pornography, British law enforcement said in court documents made public on Monday in the US.”

item.title: Contemporary conflict and ‘reimagining’ museum practice: IWM sets out new research aims
item.description: Museums Journal: “Imperial War Museums (IWM) has set out its research priorities for the next five years, including a goal of reimagining museum practice, a broader focus on ‘conflict histories that matter now’, and preparations for the second world war centenary.”

item.title: Data Expert Austin Kocher Will Launch Monthly NYC Immigration Column
item.description: Documented NY: “As covered in an earlier interview with Documented, Kocher, a data researcher, geographer and Substack writer, has spent nearly two decades studying the U.S. immigration enforcement system on the national level…. Kocher will distill and localize data to focus on New York City, with the aim of helping readers make sense of the current immigration system, through numbers.”

item.title: The L.A. people who record random sounds, from duck quacks to fax machines
item.description: Los Angeles Times: “The group is silent and still, reverently absorbing the mechanical chug of this nearly outmoded office machine like Hollywood Bowl-goers taking in Joshua Bell. When the recording ends, everyone claps enthusiastically. This is a listening session hosted by the Los Angeles Field Recording Club.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Insurance claims to test Altman and Amodei liability for ‘rogue’ AI
item.description: Financial Times: “Insurers are preparing for multimillion-dollar claims stemming from AI agents going ‘rogue’, with growing concern that top executives such as OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei could be held liable for the actions of their models.”

item.title: Have You Been Duped by an AI Recipe? Here’s Everything You Need to Know
item.description: The Kitchn: “‘Frankenstein recipes,’ a term coined by Adam, refers to a mismatched recipe you’ll find in Google’s AI overview or AI mode, which you can’t opt out of. When you search for, say, lasagna or roast chicken, Google will now often compile bits and pieces from existing recipes on the internet — ingredients from one recipe site, a cooking method from another — and mush them into one final ‘recipe.’ This is obviously a recipe for disaster (pun intended!).”

item.title: Trump Admits He’s a NIMBY on Data Centers
item.description: Gizmodo: “Donald Trump has spent recent weeks insisting that AI data centers are fantastic and every American should want to have one in their community. The president has even claimed that they make everyone rich, teasing the idea of a ‘dividend’ that could be paid out in communities where they’re built. But Trump seemed to contradict himself in a new interview published Thursday. The aspiring authoritarian leader admitted to Time magazine that he wouldn’t want to live next to a data center, echoing a common sentiment among Americans.”

item.title: The People of Utah vs. Kevin O’Leary
item.description: The Verge: “From the moment he announced the project he had proclaimed it as all but inevitable: blessed by state leadership, approved unanimously by local officials, demanded by national security, and opposed only by sinister outside forces. Now came a quiet retreat. Less than three weeks later, O’Leary and Fox were sued for defamation by Alliance for a Better Utah, Elevate Strategies, Gabrielle Finlayson, and Joshua Kanter.”

item.title: TikTok rolls out an AI shopping assistant and one-click checkout
item.description: TechCrunch: “TikTok describes its new Shopping Assistant as a conversational AI agent designed to help users discover and purchase products. The company says the assistant understands context and remembers users’ preferences and needs throughout the conversation. It offers real-time, AI-powered shopping guidance, such as product details, shipping information, sizing, availability, and help completing a purchase.”

item.title: Pentagon stops using Anthropic AI tools after blacklisting company, BBC told
item.description: BBC: “The US Department of Defence is no longer using Anthropic’s AI tools, an official has told the BBC, months after it designated the company a supply chain risk on national security grounds.”

item.title: Musicians Versus the A.I. Machine. Why Bother Writing Songs Anymore?
item.description: New York Times: “I’m Matt Richtel, a New York Times reporter, occasional songwriter and the ringleader of this experiment. The idea was straightforward: Four top-shelf, lifelong musicians and I would spend a weekend in a recording studio to write and record several songs nearly from scratch. We wanted to see whether we could do better than A.I. at making fresh music. And would it be worth our time, hassle and occasional creative dispute?”

item.title: Are Colorado’s Realtors at risk of being replaced by AI agents?
item.description: Denver Post: “AI is not new to the industry. Even human Realtors are incorporating artificial intelligence into their day-to-day operations — a move experts say is necessary if agents want to stay competitive in the rapidly evolving business. But Ridley is one of the first companies to tap into the niche of AI home-selling. The platform touts that sellers who use their service save more than $40,000 on average.”

item.title: OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’
item.description: The Guardian: “A safety leader at OpenAI has quit the company, warning that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not ‘being nearly careful enough’ about developing the technology. David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, explained his resignation in an essay headlined: ‘I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken.'”

item.title: Change.org leans into AI with $100 million investment
item.description: Axios: “Change.org was founded as a venture-backed organization, before a 2021 restructuring that saw investors like Reid Hoffman and Sam Altman donate their shares to a nonprofit structure. Now the group tells Axios that it’s investing around $100 million of its own money to rebuild its core petitions platform via AI.”

item.title: Human Contractors Are Seeing All Your Horny — and Creepy — AI Prompts
item.description: Futurism: “According to a new scoop from 404 Media, hundreds of human contractors who were hired to improve Microsoft’s Copilot AI are reviewing users’ image editing prompts and the photos that they upload. And many of these workers say they’re being inundated with dark and sexually explicit requests.”

item.title: Google wins dismissal of Chegg, Penske Media lawsuits over AI overviews
item.description: Reuters: “Alphabet’s Google has persuaded a US federal judge to dismiss lawsuits from education technology company Chegg and Rolling Stone publisher Penske Media Corp that alleged ​the search engine giant unlawfully used their content in AI-generated summaries that ‌draw readers away from their websites.”

item.title: Vibecoded Decomps Face Takedowns As Fallout And MW2 Projects Removed
item.description: The Gamer: “The projects that went viral this week were built with far more aggressive AI assistance. One of the first was Fallout: New York. ChrisFirst shared a clip on Twitter showing a browser‑playable recreation of Fallout built with Claude Opus 5.5. It had quests, dialogue trees, VATS, a working Pip‑Boy, and an entire city generated without any texture or sound files. Every building, weapon, face, and ambient noise was ‘generated by code.’ The post pulled in millions of views before ChrisFirst shared that he received a cease-and-desist from Bethesda and shut the project down.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Tippett Studios | In the wake of its closure, a digital archive of animated materials appears online
item.description: Film Stories: “August brought with it the sad news that Tippett Studios, the Berkeley-based animation and effects house founded by Phil Tippett, was closing down. The company had been in financial trouble for a while, and as it closed its doors on the 28th of that month, decades of props, memorabilia and art was sold off in a two-day auction….An anonymous person was at the auction in August, spotted a folder of CD-ROMs and other discs, and managed to acquire it for an undisclosed sum. Rather than keep the contents of those discs to themselves, that person has now uploaded it all to the Internet Archive.”

item.title: WordPress Accessibility Day: 2026
item.description: Accessible Web Design: “The first WordPress Accessibility Day was 6 years ago today. It started at 17:45 UTC on October 2nd, 2020, when I gave the opening remarks. It certainly took a very different path than the one towards the 2026 edition, which starts in just a few days, on October 7th.”

item.title: ‘Jane Doe’ solidarity posts flood social media after Cornell rape lawsuit
item.description: Associated Press: “It was one woman, then another, and another, until a trickle became a flood. Countless women, and some men, posting on social media that they were Jane Doe, in support of a young woman using that name to file a lawsuit against Cornell University and seven fraternity members she accuses of raping her.”

item.title: After Outcry, Monitors the Trump Administration Tried to Scrap Return to Sea
item.description: New York Times: “Under pressure from Congress, a network of ocean monitors that provides vital data to meteorologists, climate scientists, oceanographers and the fishing industry is being restored.”

item.title: 15 Hacks Every Opera Browser User Should Know
item.description: Lifehacker: “… the browser still retains its core philosophy of shipping useful integrated features—even if those options aren’t always obvious. From bypassing unskippable YouTube ads to using a built-in volume booster for every tab, here are the best Opera hacks you should know about.”

item.title: Japan’s digital libraries still on the rise after pandemic boom
item.description: Asahi Shimbun: “Japan’s public libraries are quietly undergoing a digital transformation. In just six years, the number of local governments offering e-book lending services has increased sevenfold, reaching 613 prefectures and municipalities and giving more than 70 percent of the population round-the-clock access to literature.”

item.title: Dutch eyewear chain Hans Anders halts sale of Meta glasses, citing privacy concerns
item.description: Reuters: “One of the largest Dutch eyewear retail chains said on Friday it had suspended sales of Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses in the Netherlands ​and Belgium amid growing privacy concerns, in one of the first such ‌moves by a retailer.”

item.title: Hackers demand ransom from Slate Valley school district after compromising teachers’ personal data
item.description: VT Digger: “Hackers are demanding hundreds of thousands of dollars in ransom from the Slate Valley Unified School District after hacking a district server last month and compromising teachers’ personal information, according to Superintendent Brooke Olsen-Farrell.”

item.title: New Initiative to Examine How Museums Engage the Communities They Serve
item.description: Association of Science and Technology Centers: “The Association of Science and Technology Centers, Garibay Group, and the Association of Children’s Museums, with support from the Institute of Museum and Library Services (Award MG-255854-OMS-24), today announced the launch of Museums Serving All People, a new initiative to study how museums build and sustain public engagement, and embed organizational values in programs, exhibits, events, and partnerships, as well as internal policies and practices.”

item.title: Polish team travels to West Point to digitally preserve Tadeusz Kościuszko’s Revolutionary War legacy
item.description: West Point: “Nearly 250 years after Tadeusz Kościuszko helped shape the defenses of West Point, a team from his native Poland is using 3D scanning, aerial photography and other digital technology to preserve the physical traces of his legacy for future generations. Three members of Poland’s Foundation for the Virtualization of National Cultural Heritage traveled approximately 4,200 miles to the U.S. Military Academy from Sept. 14-29 to digitally document Revolutionary War-era sites and artifacts associated with the Polish-American hero.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: PPP Cameras unveils new website aiming to list every film camera ever made
item.description: Kosmo Foto: “PPP Cameras’ Pierro Pozella has unveiled a momentous project – a free-to-access website which intends to list every film camera ever made. The site, called Camera Index, has already launched with more than 1,400 cameras made by manufacturers with the letter ‘A’, including Agfa, Ansco, Alpa and Argus.”

item.title: placedb
item.description: Found on Reddit: a giant dataset at From the countries list: “255 countries and territories. 4,314 states, provinces and other first-level divisions. 1,671,395 cities and towns, every one with latitude and longitude. Free to download as JSON, in the public domain, with no API key.”

item.title: CAL FIRE launches new app for real-time wildfire, emergency information
item.description: KTLA: “CAL FIRE has launched a new mobile platform designed to give Californians real-time information about wildfires and other emergencies directly from public safety agencies. The new platform, called AwareCA, was announced Thursday by CAL FIRE Chief Joe Tyler, who said the agency’s website received 100 million views in 2025, with a majority of visitors seeking information about wildfires.”

item.title: Libro.fm, Silent Book Club Plan Banned Books Week Read-In
item.description: Publishers Weekly: “From October 4–10, Libro.fm and Silent Book Club are urging audiophiles to join a Banned Books Week Read-In. More than 400 bookstores, libraries, and SBC chapters will host a social event for readers who enjoy talking to strangers as much as donning headphones and retreating into a story.”

item.title: Follow the Trail of the Bookmobile in New Issues of The Yadkin Ripple!
item.description: DigitalNC: “These newest issues date from 1941 through 1964, though DigitalNC has issues of The Yadkin Ripple from as early as 1893! Since its founding in 1892 by Mattie Johnson Hall, The Yadkin Ripple has always covered a mix of national and local news for its readership across Yadkin County.”

item.title: Google Tells Sites To Fact-Check AI Content Before Publishing
item.description: Search Engine Journal: Blinking confused man meme .gif “Google’s guidance on AI-generated content now says to fact-check it by hand before publishing, and the review extends to titles, alt text, and other metadata.”

item.title: Grant will expand Fannie Lou Hamer Digital Driving Tour
item.description: Mississippi Today: “The Jonathan Logan Family Foundation awarded $25,000 to the ‘Fannie Lou Hamer’s America’ project to support research and the production of 12 new tour stops and multimedia resources, highlighting historic locations connected to Hamer’s grassroots organizing, voting rights work, civic participation, food justice and community empowerment.”

item.title: Map Pac-Man is Back!
item.description: Maps Mania: “On April Fool’s Day 2015, a button was added to Google Maps which, when selected, turned the streets of the current map view into a fully functioning game of Pac-Man. Players could navigate the familiar streets, eating dots and avoiding ghosts just as they would in the classic arcade game. Pac-Man on Map is a tribute to that much-missed April Fool’s Day feature. The game similarly transforms real-world streets into a playable Pac-Man maze, using road data to generate a layout wherever you choose to play.”

item.title: Inclusive Content in Uncertain Times: A 2026 Annual Survey of Museum-Goers Data Story
item.description: American Alliance of Museums: “Last year, we asked whether all that political pressure on DEAI reflects a shift in public opinion. The short answer is still no. The majority of US adults, and the majority of museum-goers, support and want museums to share inclusive content. This has not changed. What has changed is the political environment.”

item.title: Mellon Foundation Releases the First National Study of Community-Based Archives
item.description: Mellon Foundation: “Today, the Mellon Foundation released ‘Powerful but Precarious: Mapping the Landscape of Community-Based Archives,’ the first national study of its kind. Produced in partnership with research firm Engage R+D, the study draws on a survey of 336 independent, community-led archives, and in-depth interviews with more than 20 practitioners across the country.”

item.title: Maine State Archives offers expanded digital access with Open Access
item.description: State of Maine: “Secretary of State Shenna Bellows today announced the official launch of Open Access, the Maine State Archives (MSA) new online platform for publicly accessible, digitized and born-digital public records. The platform can be accessed at https://digitalarchives.maine.gov or from the Maine State Archives section of the Secretary of State website.”

item.title: Archiving The World’s Oldest Webcam Feed
item.description: Hackaday: “FogCam is the oldest webcam feed that’s still up and running. Installed at San Francisco State University, it’s been slowly uploading a new image to the web every 20 to 60 seconds or so since September 30, 1994. Very few of those images have ever been saved, but [Justin Earl] has come along to fix that with Fog-Bank.” I recommend against reading the comments.

item.title: UADA news release: Who controls your farm data? NALC webinar examines emerging state laws
item.description: National Agricultural Law Center: “The webinar, titled ‘Agricultural Data Rights: A New State Law Landscape,’ will examine how new state laws are addressing agricultural data ownership and monetization rights among various participants in the agricultural technology creation and usage chain. The one-hour, online event will begin at 11 a.m. CDT on Wednesday, Oct. 21. It is free and open to the public.”

item.title: A hack of Pentagon personnel data went undetected for nine months, exposing 3 million people
item.description: TechSpot: “The Pentagon’s personnel data system was accessed for roughly nine months before officials discovered and patched the vulnerability, which exposed personally identifiable information tied to more than 3 million people. It contained a particularly sensitive combination of data: Social Security numbers and information about the jobs held by military and civilian personnel – a pairing that raises risks beyond conventional identity theft.”

item.title: Google Tests Dropping I’m Feeling Lucky Button From Search Bar
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Google seems to be testing dropping the historic I’m Feeling Lucky button for the main Google Search bar. It is totally gone for some searchers when you start to type your query, and in other cases, it is supplemented with AI buttons.”

item.title: Delaware Public Archives Celebrates American Archives Month!
item.description: State of Delaware: “The Delaware Public Archives is excited to announce that virtual reference appointments with archivists are now available on Thursdays at 10:00 a.m., 2:00 p.m., and 3:00 p.m. These virtual appointments are 30 minutes long and take place via Microsoft Teams. During the session, the reference archivist will suggest where to begin your research and provide an overview of digital materials available on the Delaware Public Archives Portal and website.”

item.title: UK rail cops’ £320K face-scanning spree nets zero matches
item.description: The Register: “British Transport Police (BTP) spent more than £320,000 putting half a million commuters through live facial recognition cameras, only for the system to identify precisely nobody it was looking for.”

item.title: I’m leaving Reddit because of RSS
item.description: Jeff Johnson: “The most ridiculous part of Reddit’s announcement was the suggestion that subreddit moderators replace RSS feeds with Discord notifications. What perversity, insanity to recommend a competing social network as the only practical way to use yours! I’m also skeptical of Reddit’s public excuse for dropping RSS: bot scraping. As I noted back in June, Reddit is already rate-limiting RSS feeds. If the current limits are insufficient, why not impose stricter limits?”

item.title: 18 Adorable Winners From the Dog Photography Awards
item.description: PetaPixel: “Picked from 1,900 entries across 50 countries, Katie Brockman from the United States took home the title of Dog Photographer of the Year for her thoughtful portrait of a pit bull.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Google freezes open-source bug bounty program amid flood of invalid AI slop submissions — product flaw submissions halted until 2027 as maintainers drown in hallucinations
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “Google has officially suspended product vulnerability submissions to its Open Source Software Vulnerability Reward Program (OSS VRP) — a bug bounty program — over an influx of invalid AI-driven reports. The company, in an official X post on October 1, encouraged participants to explore other VRP programs and committed to providing an update by the first quarter of 2027, while it reformats and works on this aspect of the program in the meantime.”

item.title: How Meta Uses A.I. Data Centers to Avoid Billions in Federal Taxes
item.description: New York Times: “Here’s what Meta is doing: For tax purposes, the company classifies its enormous, multibillion-dollar data centers as ‘pilot models.’ Under a tax credit created in the 1980s to spur innovation, companies can get a rebate for supplies, but only if they are being tested in an experimental effort, not standard business operations. Meta is claiming that the costly A.I. computer chips it buys from companies, including Nvidia, are entitled to a taxpayer-provided discount as part of the experiment. The move caused some unease within Meta’s finance department.”

item.title: Microsoft Shrivels When Asked If Its “Good Neighbor” Data Center Policy Will Involve Actually Supporting Community Groups
item.description: Futurism: “As Ars Technica reported, the group We Make Indiana — a coalition of 25 various interfaith groups, law enforcement associations, mental health organizations, and other non-profits — quickly ran up against the limits of Microsoft’s altruism after approaching a company liason to raise revenue for community services.”

item.title: How Texas Helped a Private School Chain’s AI Tool Get Into Public School Classrooms
item.description: ProPublica: “Just three months after the Texas State Board of Education raised concerns about Alpha School’s AI learning platform, Education Commissioner Mike Morath was in talks about using the tool in public schools.”

item.title: Wes Moore forms bipartisan governors group on AI, citing federal inaction
item.description: Associated Press: “Gov. Wes Moore of Maryland is forming a bipartisan group of governors to respond to mounting concerns about the threats posed by artificial intelligence as he argued that states need to fill a void left by the federal government’s inaction on the issue.”

item.title: RFK Jr. Wants to AI-ify Health Care. Claude Says He’s Full of Sh*t.
item.description: The Bulwark: “INSPIRED BY HIS CALL TO USE AI, I went ahead and asked Claude (Anthropic’s AI assistant) to analyze some of Kennedy’s more memorable statements. I used the professional, paid version, because it provides access to more capable AI models that can produce more accurate results, and I started with one of Kennedy’s favorite claims: that the scientific community hasn’t seriously investigated links between vaccines and autism.”

item.title: New Mexico to jump into frontier AI regulation
item.description: Politico: “New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez is slated to propose a state framework to regulate frontier artificial intelligence, pushing the state toward reining in the cutting edge of the fast-developing technology.”

item.title: AI learned how to write from humans. Now humans are trying not to sound like AI.
item.description: Poynter: “Artificial intelligence is making editors do strange things, like second-guess skills built over entire careers or blanch at the sight of punctuation marks. This manifested at the recent ACES: The Society for Editing’s virtual conference.”

item.title: An AI radio DJ has shot to stardom in LA Human hosts aren’t happy about it
item.description: Los Angeles Times: “GeeGee is Geraldine Guzman. Her popular partner is Coyotec — an artificial intelligence bot programmed to mimic a radio repartee. Working with a large language model has been rewarding but unpredictable, Guzman says. Coyotec comes up with unexpected takes on topics and sometimes has to be told to stop swearing.”

item.title: Meta’s Latest AI Product Is A Terrifying And Hilarious Mess
item.description: Karl Bode: “Meta claimed repeatedly that their new Muse agent was built with a heavy focus on privacy and security. But this is Meta, a soggy ad monopoly run by an unfireable authoritarian-friendly manbaby with a long history of making positively terrible choices, so things very quickly got out of control. Right out of the gate, Muse launched with a nasty zero-day flaw that created a backdoor on Mac computers, allowing a hacker to not only gain total control of the Muse AI client, but surveil you without your knowledge.”

item.title: OpenAI adds $500(!) Pro subscription, nerfs its existing $200 tier
item.description: Engadget: “Announced during the company’s DevDay event today, OpenAI’s new Pro 500 plan offers OpenAI’s highest usage allowance and comes with access to its new ‘Ultrafast’ feature — it also costs $500 per month. At the end of 2024, OpenAI became the first AI lab to introduce a $200 Pro plan. Nearly every other provider, including Anthropic and Perplexity, later announced their own $200 tiers, so it’s possible other competitors will follow suit.”

item.title: Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons
item.description: BBC: “Chinese AI developer Moonshot is conducting an internal review after researchers were able to persuade two of its popular Kimi models to tell them how to make biological weapons and carry out assassinations.”

item.title: Florida AG files to block ChatGPT development and place restrictions on OpenAI
item.description: Florida Phoenix: “Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed Monday for a temporary injunction against OpenAI and Chat GPT, upping his legal challenge against the artificial intelligence company that he says has admitted it can’t regulate its own technology. The 39-page motion asks the court to temporarily prohibit OpenAI from developing new artificial intelligence models without independent third-party safeguards and approval.”

item.title: AI tool for mapping smallholder crops proves itself in Senegal
item.description: University of Cambridge: “Researchers used Cambridge’s Tessera, an open-source AI model trained on satellite images, to map crops in Senegal’s groundnut basin. They found that Tessera was more accurate than current methods, getting the right result 84% of the time in tests while using only a fraction of computational resources and pre-labelled data. In one scenario, it performed 28% better than the next-best model.”

item.title: This AI Can Estimate How Long You’ve Been Dead. How It Works Is the Weird Part
item.description: Gizmodo: “In a study published Monday in Nature Communications, researchers developed an AI system that uses microbes on cadavers to estimate their postmortem intervals (PMI), or time since death. The system, called mHolmes, was trained on public data from 34 human cadavers. While further work is needed, it could one day greatly improve forensic investigations.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: New ‘Oligarch Index’ Tracks California’s Biggest Political Spenders
item.description: Capital & Main: “As the California Oligarch Index makes clear, a relatively tiny number of wealthy donors and corporations are exerting profound influence over who gets elected and which laws get passed in the Golden State.”

item.title: The Oʻahu Cemetery Project Preserved on Papakilo
item.description: Ka Wai Ola: “In 1986, Nanette Napoleon surveyed gravesites across 46 Oʻahu cemeteries, documenting the information recorded on tombstones and grave markers. These cemeteries were selected because they had no publicly accessible burial records at the time….The digitization of the Oʻahu Cemetery Project was a three-year endeavor that took a dozen Hawaiian Historical Society staff, volunteers, and interns to complete.”

item.title: Happy Opt Out October! Let’s Find Real Alternatives to the Tech Giants
item.description: EFF: “Last year, we created Opt Out October to help remind ourselves of the variety of ways we can take back control of our data through small steps inside apps, operating systems, and other various forms. This year, we highlight the idea that sometimes the best way to control your data is to leave a platform, app, or operating system altogether. To do so, we’ve created a hub of resources sharing ways to find new software that isn’t made by the tech giants, take advantage of the growing universe of new social media options, install a whole new operating system, and better control how various popular tools and software use your data for AI training.”

item.title: Reddit is putting more limits on Old.Reddit.com
item.description: Ars Technica: “Soon, Reddit won’t let people use Old.Reddit.com unless they have used the site while logged in within the previous six months. In July, Reddit started requiring that users be logged in to access Old Reddit. This new requirement is an effort to reduce Reddit’s biggest source of scraping and automated traffic, the company says.”

item.title: Canonical begins pushing Resolute Raccoon
item.description: The Register: “Resolute Raccoon is ready to roll out to existing Ubuntu users. Canonical has flipped the switch, and users on 24.04 will start to get offered 26.04.1. Canonical has marked the occasion with an official announcement that it’s time to upgrade your desktop.”

item.title: Google Maps Now Requires Sign In To Read All Reviews & More
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Google Maps now requires you to sign in to a Google account to see all the reviews on a Google Business Profile listing. It is also required in order to sort the reviews, leave a review, and more. I assume this was done to help prevent AI, bots, and third parties from scraping the Google reviews.”

item.title: Benin: National Library prepares digital library and strategic plan for 2027-2033
item.description: Benin Web TV: “The National Library of Benin is preparing several initiatives aimed at modernizing the management and access to documentary heritage. The institution is specifically working on a national digital library, a comprehensive national bibliography, a statistical platform for the book chain, and a strategic plan covering the period from 2027 to 2033.”

item.title: Forbidden Stories and UC Berkeley Journalism join forces to launch a flagship, cross-border investigative lab and respond to mounting threats to press freedom in the U.S.
item.description: UC Berkeley Journalism: “The Forbidden Stories Lab based at the UC Berkeley School of Journalism will mobilize newsrooms across the United States and internationally to pursue and amplify public-interest investigations facing threats or attempts to silence them.”

item.title: NSA Launches 13th Annual Codebreaker Challenge
item.description: NSA: “The National Security Agency (NSA) officially announced the launch of its 13th Annual Codebreaker Challenge today, inviting college and university students across the United States to test their technical skills against a realistic, mission-centric cybersecurity scenario.”

item.title: Kansas Legislature’s budget cuts compel Fort Hays State University to close Sternberg Museum
item.description: Kansas Reflector: “[Fort Hays State University president Tisa] Mason said in a 1,500-word statement that Fort Hays State received a $2.4 million reduction in state funding during the 2026 session. In addition, the Legislature requested FHSU assess how it would slash administrative costs by 10%. The university has relied for decades on revenue from higher education programs in China, but restrictions by the state could jeopardize as much as $6 million in funding.”

item.title: Australian Museum partners with Warlpiri Project on community-led repatriation of sacred objects
item.description: Australian Museum: “The Australian Museum (AM) has returned 17 culturally significant sacred objects to Warlpiri ownership, marking an important milestone in a community-led repatriation process built on research, cultural authority and partnership.”

item.title: People Are Sequencing Mushroom DNA at Home Now
item.description: Bay Nature: “Today, the search for fungal answers has taken over [Harte] Singer’s life—and his garage in Santa Rosa, which he’s now converted into a full laboratory dedicated to fungal DNA. … He is completing a master’s degree in mycology at California State University East Bay, runs his own fungal DNA sequencing business, and leads sequencing for the California Fungal Diversity Survey (CA FUNDIS)—a community science project that aims to collect, preserve, and sequence as much of the state’s dizzying fungal diversity as possible.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: In the Moment: Oral History as a Democratic Resource
item.description: Charles F Kettering Foundation: “…the Kettering Foundation’s Democracy and the Arts focus area is partnering with OurStoryBridge to create the Democracy & the Arts oral history collection. These stories are from people experiencing challenges imposed by current efforts to limit free speech and creative expression in the arts and humanities. This collection is part of the broader OurStoryBridgeListens: Present in the Moment initiative that documents how Americans are experiencing democracy through their own voices.”

item.title: This free website lets you see what your Parisian neighborhood looked like in 1970
item.description: Paris Secret: “A street filled with cars, a storefront that no longer exists, a construction site at the base of a building, or simply Parisians pausing in front of a café. The Paris 1970 website offers a fascinating glimpse into the capital as it was more than half a century ago, featuring tens of thousands of photographs taken throughout the city.”

item.title: Padilla, Schiff, Durbin, Duckworth Introduce Legislation to Protect Regional National Archives Facilities from Closure
item.description: Block Club Chicago: “Today, U.S. Senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff (both D-Calif.), Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), and Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), introduced the National Archives Protection Act, legislation that would require congressional approval before the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) can close or significantly restrict access to existing regional facilities.”

item.title: NEWS RELEASE: DBEDT Releases 2025 State of Hawai’i Data Book
item.description: State of Hawaii: “The Hawaiʻi State Data Book remains the state’s most comprehensive statistical resource, featuring 24 sections and 832 data tables covering population, education, environment, economics, energy, real estate, construction, business enterprises, government, tourism and transportation.”

item.title: A comprehensive list to picking your webcomic or webnovel’s home.
item.description: K-Comics Beat: “This is a list of various sites you can host your webcomic or webnovel, in no particular order. It is organized into four main categories: Comic hosting sites, Site builders, blog sites that can be repurposed or have support for webcomics and webnovels, and webcomic rings and databases. I will also mention whether these platforms do have support for mature/NSFW content, as well as if these platforms utilize AI in some form, since these are variables many creatives consider for their projects.” I’m not very familiar with this space so I can’t tell you whether this article is comprehensive, but it IS extensive.

item.title: Social media influencer Brooke Eby dies at 37 after battle with ALS
item.description: NBC Chicago: “Eby created a community on TikTok — gathering hundreds of thousands of followers — with the goal of helping to change how others understand ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease. On Thursday, she died from complications of ALS at the age of 37, according to the ALS Network.”

item.title: Wikipedia Fans Worry the Site Is Getting a Bad Deal From Its Streetwear Brand Collab
item.description: Gizmodo: “Fans, definitionally, tend to like it when their favs get tapped for fun, trendy projects. But when the object of your fandom is a notoriously cash-strapped online resource, one can’t help but paternalistically try to see the fine print on the deal—like the recently announced one between Wikipedia and the streetwear brand Online Ceramics—before celebrations begin.”

item.title: Fake QR codes on Manhattan parking meters lead to identity theft charges
item.description: Gothamist: “Mihai Theodor Enescu was arraigned in Manhattan Supreme Court on five counts of second-degree identity theft and six counts of second-degree criminal impersonation, court records show. Prosecutors allege he was behind the phony city payment website linked from the QR code stickers, which asked users for credit card information.”

item.title: Librarians on Libraries
item.description: New York Times: “We spoke with dozens of librarians at the A.L.A. conference this summer in Chicago. They came from rural towns and major cities, elementary schools and universities, local branches and big government agencies. These librarians want you to know that they don’t sit around reading all day. They want you to know about book bans and budget cuts, but also about career counseling and crafting groups and pop-up medical clinics.”

item.title: DCHS Awarded $5400 Digitization Grant
item.description: Disciples of Christ Historical Society: “We are pleased to announce that the JSTOR Digital Collections Initiative awarded the Disciples of Christ Historical Society a $5400 digitization grant. The grant, made possible by a JSTOR and Mellon Foundation partnership, aims to help JSTOR Digital Stewardship Charter Program members make more digitized archival and special collections materials available to researchers.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Misleading Google AI instructions cause Kodiak woman to be cited for illegal snipe hunt
item.description: Alaska Beacon: “Incorrect information provided by a Google AI overview caused a Kodiak woman to hunt snipe illegally on Sept. 5, according to a citation filed this week at the Kodiak district court. Writing in an affidavit attached to the citation, Alaska Wildlife Trooper Alex Wick said [Christina] Weaver called troopers to self-report the violation.”

item.title: Protests against OpenAI get increasingly creative
item.description: Ars Technica: “Two artists from a Bay Area studio unveiled What Iceberg?, a table-sized installation placed at the public entrance to an OpenAI developer event in San Francisco on Tuesday. According to a description of the piece, the 5-foot-tall sculpture ‘shows OpenAI’s leaders and investors escaping a sinking ship with unimaginable wealth, while everyone else is left to face the cost of AI.'”

item.title: Amazon to invest $1B into data center communities amid backlash against data center rollouts
item.description: Associated Press: “Amazon is investing more than $1 billion over the next five years into communities where it operates data centers for education, job training, water and energy preservation projects and other local priorities as it reacts to a growing backlash from politicians and consumers to the tech industry’s rollout of the massive buildings.”

item.title: Siracusano to sue Vannacci over AI-manipulated revealing photo
item.description: ANSA English: “Relations with Parliament Undersecretary Matilde Siracusano said Monday that she intends to take legal action against general-turned-politician Roberto Vannacci over an AI-manipulated image of her with a revealing neckline that he posted on social media.”

item.title: Mississippi River mayors, including three in Arkansas, propose AI data center guardrails
item.description: Arkansas Times: “There are already more than 3,000 active data centers throughout the United States, including in Minnesota, Iowa, Illinois, Missouri and Tennessee. As the need for artificial intelligence and data storage grows, more cities and counties are being approached by companies interested in building data centers in their communities.”

item.title: New CT AI, data privacy laws go into effect Oct. 1. What to know
item.description: CT Mirror: “The legislation, also known as the Connecticut Artificial Intelligence Responsibility and Transparency, or CART, Act, was result of a long-sought compromise between lawmakers in the state Senate, House and governor’s office. While some of CART Act’s provisions went into effect already, some will become law starting Oct. 1.”

item.title: AI fabrication suspected of writing dozens of articles in Canadian publications
item.description: The Globe and Mail: “The explosive e-mail landed in llker Sezer’s inbox just after 9 p.m. on Sept. 2 with the subject line ‘Investigative feature submission. Canada-based criminal network with a Turkey trail.’ The story sounded like a huge scoop for Mr. Sezer and his staff of 30 journalists at Türkiye Today, an English-language news website based in Istanbul.

item.title: Meta Goes All-In On AI for Businesses Before Muse Goes Horribly Wrong
item.description: Gizmodo: “Meta is on a mission ‘to bring personal superintelligence to everyone,’ as CEO Mark Zuckerberg put it last year. We got our first glimpse of what that vision looks like earlier this month: a deceptively cutesy, Tamagotchi-like personal AI agent called Muse. On Monday, the company announced it’s also bringing its superintelligence ambitions to the all-important enterprise market with the launch of a new internal business unit.”

item.title: AI learned how to write from humans. Now humans are trying not to sound like AI.
item.description: Poynter: “Artificial intelligence is making editors do strange things, like second-guess skills built over entire careers or blanch at the sight of punctuation marks.”

item.title: China fuels rush to turn AI video into an industry
item.description: Reuters: “When Zhu Zhili was looking for a base to set up an artificial intelligence film studio in China two years ago, there was just one clear choice: the southern city ​of Shenzhen with its vast tech ecosystem. This year, AI filmmaker Zhu said he has fielded calls from officials in cities and industrial parks across China, all with the same pitch: ‌bring your AI film business here.”

item.title: People Who Drink Their Own Pee Are Obsessed With AI, Using It to Reassure Themselves That It’s a Miraculous Cure-All
item.description: Futurism: “despite some initial hurdles, acolytes of the urine drinking lifestyle have found it remarkably easy to break through chatbot safeguards — engineering AI to say whatever it is they wanted to hear to begin with, essentially. The bypass, it seems, involves simply mentioning the word ‘esoteric.'”

item.title: OpenAI Ignored Employees Who Warned It Wasn’t Doing Enough About Security
item.description: New York Times: “In emails, the employees said they worried that OpenAI’s newest artificial intelligence models were not being appropriately monitored during testing to gauge the technology’s sophistication and to secure the models, according to messages viewed by The New York Times. In response, OpenAI executives told the employees that the tests needed to move forward as quickly as possible to release the A.I. models on time. No additional security protocols were instituted, said the workers, who were not authorized to speak publicly on sensitive matters.”

item.title: Rogue OpenAI agents covered up their tracks, report says
item.description: AFP: “Artificial intelligence agents developed by OpenAI tried to erase traces of their activity after gaining unauthorized access to government websites, according to a report published Thursday. Cybersecurity firm Asymmetric Security analyzed the activity of the agents — AI programs capable of acting autonomously — which targeted Australian government websites and other public bodies between March and September.”

item.title: How Pew Research Center is – and is not – using AI in our work
item.description: Pew (PEW PEW PEW PEW PEW PEW!): “As public-facing social scientists committed to innovation, we’re exploring what AI might add to our toolkit. As public opinion researchers, we’re studying and explaining how people are reacting to the advance of AI technologies. And as information providers whose fundamental values include accuracy and methodological rigor, we’re moving with great deliberation to ensure the quality of our work remains high. In all of these spaces, our primary commitment is that our work remains people-centered.” Good evening, Internet…
